title: El Niño Bakes Southeast Asia
gist: The 2026 El Niño may be the strongest in 140 years and lands on Southeast Asia — source of the world's #2 and #3 rice exporters, 85 percent of palm oil, and the #2 and #4 coffee producers — on top of an Iran-war price shock, with Bangkok rice already at $490/ton (+27.5 percent YTD) and regional yields projected down 2-8 percent through 2028. The brief also maps Indonesia's haze-fire risk, Malaysia's hardening line on the Rohingya, and the US Pax Silica / AI Spark push against China for Southeast Asia's chip and critical-minerals base.

insights.claim: The 2026 El Niño may be the strongest in 140 years and is predicted to run until spring 2027, meaning food supply and price effects persist into 2028.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: This is a multi-year soft-commodity supply story, not a single-season spike — structure agricultural exposure across 2027-2028 rather than the next harvest.
insights.quote: El Niño is predicted to last up until spring 2027, which means that effects on food supply and prices will persist into 2028.
insights.locator: El Niño Hits Hard

insights.claim: Insurer Munich Re identifies Asia-Pacific as the worst-affected region for this El Niño, with heat waves, drought, wildfires and increased typhoon risk.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: Reinsurer loss expectations concentrate in Asia-Pacific; watch cat-bond pricing and Asian property/crop insurance combined ratios.
insights.quote: The Asia-Pacific will be the worst-affected region, according to insurance giant Munich Re, with heat waves, drought, wildfires, and increased typhoon risk.
insights.locator: El Niño Hits Hard

insights.claim: This El Niño arrives before the region's agricultural sector has recovered from the 2023-2024 event, whose legacy of increased farmer debt is still being felt.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: Back-to-back shocks with no balance-sheet recovery raise rural credit-loss risk for Southeast Asian agricultural lenders and microfinance.
insights.locator: This year’s El Niño follows another strong El Niño event

insights.claim: The El Niño shock compounds an existing regional price surge caused by the Iran war, and the author has previously flagged high food prices as a driver of political instability in Southeast Asia.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: Compounding energy and food inflation in emerging Asia is the classic setup for protests and government instability — a political-risk overlay on ASEAN equity and FX exposure.
insights.quote: The region is already facing higher prices as result of the Iran war, and El Niño will only intensify that.
insights.locator: El Niño Hits Hard

insights.claim: Thailand and Vietnam are the world's second and third-largest rice exporters, making Southeast Asian drought a direct transmission channel into global rice prices.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: Rice-importing economies across Africa and the Middle East face imported food inflation; watch for export bans, which historically amplify the spike.
insights.quote: Thailand and Vietnam are the world’s second and third-largest exporters of rice.
insights.locator: The effects on Southeast Asia will also be felt

insights.claim: Indonesia and Malaysia produce 85 percent of the world's palm oil, and palm oil alongside rice is described as particularly sensitive to climate anomalies.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: An 85 percent two-country concentration in palm oil means El Niño is effectively a single-point-of-failure risk for global vegetable-oil supply and downstream food and biofuel costs.
insights.quote: Indonesia and Malaysia produce 85 percent of the world’s palm oil.
insights.locator: The effects on Southeast Asia will also be felt

insights.claim: Vietnam and Indonesia are the world's second and fourth-largest coffee producers, adding a third major soft commodity to the El Niño exposure list.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: Robusta supply risk stacks on top of rice and palm oil — a broad soft-commodity basket long rather than a single-name trade.
insights.quote: Vietnam and Indonesia are the world’s second and fourth-largest producers of coffee.
insights.locator: The effects on Southeast Asia will also be felt

insights.claim: Regional rice yields are estimated to fall between 2 and 8 percent, a wide band that reflects genuine uncertainty about the severity of the shock.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: The 8 percent tail is where export restrictions get triggered; position size for the tail, not the midpoint.
insights.quote: Experts have estimated that rice yields in the region could fall between 2 to 8 percent.
insights.locator: The effects on Southeast Asia will also be felt

insights.claim: Thailand received roughly 60 percent less rain than normal between January and April 2026, and its national water agency warns of a drought crisis worse than the 2015 El Niño year.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
entities: Office of the National Water Resources
insights.so_what: A 60 percent rainfall deficit is already locked in for the current crop — Thai rice export volumes for the coming season are impaired regardless of what happens next.
insights.quote: Thailand received roughly 60 percent less rain than normal between January and April.
insights.locator: Some effects are already being felt.

insights.claim: Bangkok export rice reached $490 per metric ton at the end of June, up 27.5 percent since the start of 2026, giving a hard mark on how much of the shock is already priced.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: A concrete benchmark to track: further moves above $490/ton signal the drought is exceeding the 2-8 percent yield-loss base case.
insights.quote: The Bangkok export price for rice reached $490 per metric ton at the end of June, up 27.5 percent since the start of 2026.
insights.locator: Some effects are already being felt.

insights.claim: Krungthai, a major Thai bank, projects El Niño could shave 0.5 percent from Thailand's GDP in a worst-case scenario, quantifying the macro drag of the drought.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: A 50bp GDP hit is material for Thai rate expectations and the baht — factor it into Bank of Thailand policy path assumptions.
insights.quote: Research by Krungthai, a major Thai bank, projected that El Niño could shave 0.5 percent from Thailand’s GDP in a worst-case scenario.
insights.locator: Thailand’s Office of the National Water Resources has warned

insights.claim: The Philippines faces a potential 30 percent reduction in rice production from the combined El Niño and Iran-war shock, by far the most severe country-level estimate in the region.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: The Philippines is already the world's largest rice importer; a 30 percent domestic shortfall would force massive import demand into an already tight global market.
insights.quote: El Niño and the Iran war shock could reduce rice production by 30 percent.
insights.locator: In the Philippines, water reserves are already showing signs of strain.

insights.claim: More than 100,000 hectares of Cambodian rice fields have already been hit by drought according to the government.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: Confirms the shock is regional and concurrent, not confined to Thailand — reduces the odds of intra-ASEAN supply substitution smoothing prices.
insights.locator: In neighboring Cambodia, more than 100,000 hectares

insights.claim: Indonesia is the relative outlier, with its meteorological agency BMKG projecting rice production falls of just 2.6 percent even as roughly half the country sees a longer-than-normal dry season.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: Indonesia's relative insulation on rice makes it a differentiated ASEAN exposure — but the fire and haze channel, not the crop channel, is where its risk sits.
insights.quote: It predicted that rice production will fall by just 2.6 percent, though eastern parts of the country are expected to be more affected.
insights.locator: Indonesia has experienced drought in key population centers

insights.claim: The Singapore Institute of International Affairs issued a red alert for haze risk in June, a warning it last gave in 2023 when haze duly occurred, making it a validated leading indicator.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: A red alert with a demonstrated 2023 track record is actionable: expect transboundary haze disruption to Singapore and Malaysian aviation, tourism and outdoor labor.
insights.locator: In a June report, the Singapore Institute of International Affairs

insights.claim: Indonesia is worse positioned to fight fires than under the previous president, with strained firefighting budgets and an uptick in deforestation over the past two years flagged by SIIA.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: Weaker state fire-suppression capacity converts drought into actual burn area — the mechanism that turns a haze warning into a realized regional economic hit.
insights.locator: Buried in the report are some politely phrased concerns

themes.theme: Malaysia's Rohingya reversal and ASEAN drift

insights.claim: Malaysia has agreed to return 5,000 Rohingya asylum-seekers to Myanmar, whose government committed genocide against them, with Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announcing it at a campaign rally after his coalition was defeated in a state election.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: Domestic electoral weakness is driving Malaysian foreign policy toward nativism — a template for how ASEAN governments trade principle for votes under economic stress.
insights.locator: Rohingya deported to Myanmar

insights.claim: Malaysia's deportation deal, justified by 'good relations with Myanmar,' may mark the end of its role as one of ASEAN's hardest-line members against the Myanmar junta alongside Singapore and Indonesia.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: Erosion of ASEAN's isolation of the junta reduces sanctions pressure on Myanmar and could reopen commercial access to its resources.
insights.locator: My key question is if this heralds a shift

insights.claim: Junta leader Min Aung Hlaing's push for diplomatic acceptance is succeeding, with an official Bangkok visit and a prior meeting between Myanmar's foreign minister and ASEAN foreign ministers, and the Red Cross visit to Aung San Suu Kyi timed to support it.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
entities: International Committee of the Red Cross
insights.so_what: Normalization of the junta is a live trend; it changes the sanctions and reputational calculus for firms with Myanmar-adjacent supply chains.
insights.locator: Aung San Suu Kyi Alive.

themes.theme: US-China AI competition in Southeast Asia

insights.claim: The US AI push in Southeast Asia has two prongs: Pax Silica, building a China-free supply chain from critical minerals through chip fabs, data centers and models, and AI Spark, supporting government deployment of US AI models in the public sector.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: Two distinct procurement channels — hardware/supply chain versus government software contracts — to track separately when sizing US AI vendors' international revenue opportunity.
insights.locator: In Focus: America’s AI bid in Southeast Asia

insights.claim: Southeast Asia hosts five of the ten global economies best positioned in semiconductor production — Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam — plus abundant critical minerals, making it the decisive theater for AI supply-chain competition.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: Half the world's top-ten semiconductor positions sit in one hedging region — a concentration risk for any China-free supply chain that assumes ASEAN alignment.
insights.quote: The region hosts five of the 10 global economies with the best positions in semiconductor production: Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam.
insights.locator: Southeast Asia is an attractive target for these policies.

insights.claim: Pax Silica has attracted only two Southeast Asian members, the Philippines and Singapore, while AI Spark has zero announced participants, showing the US initiatives are far behind their announcements.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: Adoption is the metric that matters, not announcements — the gap suggests US AI diplomacy in ASEAN is not yet converting into contracts.
insights.locator: For Pax Silica, two Southeast Asian countries

insights.claim: US unreliability, exemplified by the sudden ban on overseas use of cutting-edge models even by allies, is itself the main obstacle to Southeast Asian alignment with Washington's AI bloc.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: Export-control volatility is destroying the US vendor value proposition abroad — a structural share gift to Chinese open-source models in non-sensitive workloads.
insights.locator: As with China’s bid for AI leadership

insights.claim: Analysts expect a bifurcated market where US models are preferred for sensitive government applications while cheaper Chinese open-source models take the lower-security workloads.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: The volume tier goes to Chinese open source and the margin tier to US vendors — a structurally smaller but higher-value addressable market for Western AI labs in ASEAN.
insights.locator: As for AI Spark, the details remain vague

insights.claim: Jacob Helberg, US undersecretary of state for economic affairs and a Palantir alum, denounces digital sovereignty as a quixotic waste of resources — a direct clash with ASEAN governments who prize the concept.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: Washington attacking digital sovereignty head-on is a self-inflicted diplomatic wound in a region that treats it as non-negotiable; expect ASEAN to hedge harder.
insights.quote: Ironically, to my ear, Hellberg’s proposals sound like Chinese President Xi Jinping’s on AI: a cooperative order, but one in which his country is a clear top dog.
